authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: Which explanation is a complete strategy justification rather than a pattern label or complexity claim?
constraints: The task evaluates the quality of the explanation.
A complete justification must address correctness and cost.
The boundary of applicability must be explicit.

options.text: Use prefix sums because each query becomes O(1) instead of O(n); the lower per-query complexity is sufficient to justify the strategy.
Use prefix sums because repeated range queries match that pattern; cumulative storage is the conventional approach and therefore needs no separate boundary analysis.
Preprocessing is permitted; cumulative sums let subtraction isolate each static range; total cost is O(n + q) time and O(n) space; frequent updates would change the choice.

feedback.reason: A complete justification connects the decision signal to a legal mechanism, correctness invariant, full cost model, and the boundary where the choice stops applying.

blocks.text: Strategy justification is not a restatement of the selected option. The strongest explanation identifies why preprocessing is legal, what state is stored, why the range formula returns exactly the requested aggregate, how setup and query costs combine, and which workload change would break the decision. A pattern label omits the proof, while a per-query comparison hides setup and memory. The transfer rule is to make every strategy choice auditable through the chain signal → mechanism → invariant → cost → boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pattern_label: The label may name a plausible family, but it does not establish legality, correctness, or cost for this contract. It becomes useful only as shorthand after the underlying reasoning is stated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.complexity_only: This compares one phase and assumes correctness and free preprocessing. It becomes complete only after setup, space, update lifetime, and the range-recovery invariant are included.

items.prompt: An immutable API allowlist must answer a high volume of exact token checks. The response is only allow or deny, order is irrelevant, and O(n) extra memory fits. Which justification for a hash set is strongest?
constraints: Many exact membership queries occur.
Arbitrary output order is acceptable.
O(n) extra memory fits.
Expected-time guarantees are acceptable unless stated otherwise.

options.text: Presence-only queries need stored keys; build the set in expected O(n), answer in expected O(1), use O(n) space, and reconsider if ordered output or deterministic bounds are required.
Use a hash set because lookup structures are designed for membership, usually run in constant time, and are the standard answer for repeated key queries.
Build a hash set because the complete workload is expected O(n + q), which is asymptotically better than scanning and therefore settles the choice by itself.

feedback.reason: The complete justification aligns the output primitive, retained state, expected cost, memory allowance, and guarantee boundary.

blocks.text: Presence queries require neither rank nor original positions, so a set contains sufficient information. Its lifecycle includes one expected O(n) build and q expected O(1) lookups, using O(n) additional entries. That rationale depends on acceptable expected-time semantics and an order-insensitive result; a deterministic ordered structure may be preferable under different contracts. The transfer rule is to justify a data structure by the exact operation it supports and the guarantees the workload requires.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_fast: This slogan names neither the required operation nor the assumptions behind performance. It becomes an acceptable summary only after the full state, cost, and boundary have been established elsewhere.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_linear: The build cost alone ignores query count, extra memory, expected-versus-worst-case semantics, and output ordering. A complexity class cannot erase functional constraints.

items.prompt: A sorted array is searched for values at two distinct positions summing to T, using pointers at both ends. Which statement supplies the decisive correctness justification?
constraints: The array is sorted.
The output asks whether two distinct positions form a pair with sum T.
Pointers begin at opposite ends.

options.text: If the sum is below T, even the largest remaining partner cannot rescue the left endpoint, so advance left; use the symmetric argument when the sum is above T.
The array is sorted and the task concerns a pair sum, so the familiar opposite-end two-pointer pattern is sufficient justification for each movement.
Each pointer moves at most n positions and never moves backward, so the linear operation count proves that every possible pair is handled correctly.

feedback.reason: The endpoint-elimination argument explains why each irreversible pointer move preserves every possible solution.

blocks.text: Maintain left < right so the pointers always denote distinct positions. Sorted order makes the current left value the smallest and the current right value the largest among remaining candidates. When their sum is below T, pairing the left value with any other remaining value cannot reach T because every other partner is no larger than the current right value; advancing left is safe. A too-large sum yields the symmetric proof for the right endpoint. The linear movement count derives time only after this invariant establishes correctness. The transfer rule is to justify every pointer move by naming the entire class of candidates it safely discards.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers_linear: This proves an operation bound for the chosen motion, not that the motion preserves solutions. It becomes relevant after the endpoint-elimination invariant is established.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_keyword: Sorted input enables several strategies and does not by itself determine the output relation. Opposite-end movement is justified only when comparison with T eliminates an endpoint.

items.prompt: A static array uses prefix sums P where P[i] is the sum of the first i elements. Which explanation correctly justifies answering range [l, r] as P[r + 1] - P[l]?
constraints: P[k] sums the first k elements.
The array is static during queries.
Ranges use inclusive endpoints [l, r].

options.text: Use P[r + 1] - P[l] because it is the standard prefix-sum formula; the conventional notation is enough to settle indexing and correctness.
Both prefixes contain every contribution before l, so subtraction cancels that shared part and leaves l through r; one O(n) build supports O(1) queries until updates occur.
The formula is correct because it performs one subtraction in constant time, making it faster than visiting the elements in the requested range.

feedback.reason: The cancellation invariant proves the range formula, while the lifecycle statement explains its cost and static-data boundary.

blocks.text: With a half-open prefix convention, P[k] stores the sum of indices 0 through k-1. P[r+1] and P[l] share every contribution before l, and subtracting removes exactly that shared prefix, leaving the requested inclusive range. The stored representation costs O(n) to build and remains valid only while the underlying values do not change or are maintained consistently. Constant-time subtraction is the consequence, not the proof. The transfer rule is to state the representation invariant and derive the query operation from it rather than quoting a memorized formula.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memorized_formula: A formula without its indexing convention is vulnerable to off-by-one errors and does not explain why it works. It becomes acceptable shorthand only when the invariant is already fixed and shared.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_fast: Execution speed does not establish semantic correctness. Subtraction is useful only because the representation makes unwanted contributions cancel exactly.

items.prompt: A candidate binary-searches the minimum capacity C for which a scheduling feasibility check succeeds. Which statement is the required justification?
constraints: The capacity domain is ordered and bounded.
The task asks for the minimum feasible capacity.
Feasibility can be checked for a proposed capacity.
A feasible upper bound has been established; otherwise the algorithm reports that no feasible capacity exists in the domain.

options.text: A feasible upper bound exists; if C is feasible, every larger capacity is feasible; feasibility therefore has one boundary, and each check safely discards half of the bounded domain.
Capacity is an ordered integer, so midpoint checks can always move toward the minimum even without proving how feasibility behaves at larger values.
The method is correct because it runs only logarithmically many feasibility checks and keeps narrowing the numeric interval until one value remains.

feedback.reason: Binary search on an answer requires a monotonic feasibility boundary. That implication, not the numeric domain or check count, licenses half discard.

blocks.text: The search domain is possible capacity values rather than array indices. A verified feasible upper bound ensures the bounded domain actually contains an answer; otherwise the no-solution case must be returned explicitly. The decisive property is upward closure: once a capacity can schedule the workload, adding capacity cannot make it infeasible. Thus false values precede true values, and a feasibility result identifies which half cannot contain the minimum. The total cost is the number of checks times the cost of one check, and strict interval shrinkage establishes termination. The transfer rule is to prove existence or handle absence, then write the one-direction implication before binary-searching any optimization parameter.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_domain: Numbers provide an order but not a monotonic predicate. This becomes sufficient only when feasibility is proven to change in one direction over that order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_checks: A short sequence of checks can still discard the true answer incorrectly. The logarithmic count is a cost result after the half-discard proof.

items.prompt: Order the components of a complete final strategy justification.
constraints: All five components are required.
Ordering is scored by preserved adjacent relations.
The final component must expose a transfer boundary.

elements.text: Name the decisive requirement or constraint signal.
Explain the state or transformation the strategy uses.
State why each operation preserves or narrows the correct answer.
Derive total time, extra space, and relevant guarantee assumptions.
State the condition under which the strategy would stop applying or another candidate would win.

feedback.reason: A justification begins with why the strategy is relevant, proves how it works, derives what it costs, and ends with its applicability boundary.

blocks.text: A complete justification is reconstructable in this dependency order:

items: Name the decisive requirement or constraint signal so the choice is tied to this problem rather than a pattern label.
Explain the state or transformation the strategy creates and how each operation uses it.
State the invariant that proves operations preserve the answer and every irreversible discard is safe.
Derive setup, operation, output, time and extra-space costs together with expected, amortized or worst-case assumptions.
Name the changed precondition, workload or resource limit that would invalidate the mechanism or let another candidate win.

blocks.text: The sequence moves from relevance through mechanism and correctness to cost, then ends with a transfer boundary instead of overgeneralization. Adjacent-relation scoring reflects those dependencies rather than treating the five statements as independent buzzwords.

items.prompt: An algorithm sorts the input to enable a linear scan, but the API promises to preserve the caller's order. Which addition makes the strategy justification complete?

options.text: Explain whether sorting a copy is affordable or whether the strategy is invalid under the mutation contract.
Omit the issue because asymptotic time is more important than input ownership.
Claim that sorting and restoring original order has no additional cost.
Rename the input as a working array so mutation no longer counts.

feedback.reason: A strategy must satisfy the output and side-effect contract as well as the computational objective.

blocks.text: Sorting can be a sound preprocessing strategy when mutation is allowed or when a copy fits the space budget. If the caller's order must remain unchanged and copying is too expensive, the proposed strategy does not meet the problem contract. Renaming a reference does not remove the side effect, and restoring order adds real work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_order: Input preservation is a correctness requirement, not an optional optimization detail.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_restore_free: Copying, sorting, and restoring have time and possibly space costs that must be included.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rename_input: Names do not change aliasing or observable mutation.

items.prompt: A proposed hash-map solution claims O(n) time for exact membership queries. Which qualification belongs in the strategy justification?

options.text: State that the bound is expected under the hash-table assumptions and separately account for memory and any adversarial worst case.
Claim hashing is worst-case constant time for every key distribution and implementation.
Ignore collisions because the map abstraction hides them from the proof.
Treat O(n) extra space as proof that lookup time is O(1).

feedback.reason: Complexity claims depend on the data-structure guarantee being used, and expected hashing is not an unconditional worst-case theorem.

blocks.text: A strong explanation identifies the map operations, their expected cost under the chosen hash assumptions, the number of operations, and the O(n) auxiliary state. If worst-case guarantees or adversarial keys matter, a different structure or hashing policy may be required. Hiding collisions does not make their cost disappear.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_always_constant: Typical hash-table lookup is expected O(1), while worst-case behavior depends on collisions and implementation guarantees.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_collisions: The complexity argument must state the assumption under which collisions remain controlled.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.space_is_time: Memory size and operation time are independent dimensions of the contract.

items.prompt: A candidate explanation says only “this is O(n log n), so it is correct.” What essential reasoning is missing?

options.text: A state invariant or elimination argument showing that the operations preserve the required answer and do not discard a needed candidate.
More runtime measurements on one input size; measurements replace a correctness proof.
Shorter names so the asymptotic argument is easier to read.
A larger hidden constant to make the complexity claim safer.

feedback.reason: Complexity measures resource use; it does not establish that the returned result satisfies the problem contract.

blocks.text: The justification must connect the chosen state to the answer: what does each entry mean, which candidates are removed, and why are those removals safe? Only after correctness is established should time, space, and assumptions be derived. A fast algorithm can consistently compute the wrong result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.more_benchmarks: Empirical speed does not prove correctness for all valid inputs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shorter_variable_names: Readability can help review but does not supply an invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.larger_constant: A constant-factor change cannot turn a missing correctness argument into a proof.

items.prompt: Select all statements that belong in the boundary section of a strategy justification.

options.text: State that a simple sum-based window rule may fail when signed values remove monotonicity.
State that a sorted two-pointer elimination proof does not transfer to arbitrary unsorted input without another invariant.
State that the strategy applies whenever the problem title contains the pattern name.
State that the fastest asymptotic candidate always wins regardless of output and mutation contracts.

feedback.reason: A transfer boundary identifies the changed premise that invalidates the proof or makes another strategy more appropriate.

blocks.text: Signed values can break a shrink monotonicity argument, and unsorted input can remove the endpoint-elimination theorem used by a sorted pair scan. Pattern labels and asymptotic speed are not universal licenses; the actual constraints, invariants, output, and side effects decide applicability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_pattern: Names do not supply the structural preconditions required by the algorithm.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.complexity_always_wins: A candidate that violates correctness or side-effect contracts is not a valid strategy, regardless of asymptotic cost.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.signed_values_break_window: The window proof depends on how boundary removal changes the maintained measure.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.unsorted_breaks_pair: The sorted-order implication is the reason an endpoint can be discarded; without it the move needs a new proof.

items.prompt: What is the strongest concise justification for selecting an O(n log n) sort-and-scan over an O(n) hash approach?
constraints: The hash approach requires expected O(1) operations.
The environment requires deterministic worst-case behavior and permits sorting.

options.text: Sorting meets the deterministic worst-case and memory contract; the expected-time hash alternative does not provide the required guarantee.
options.explanation: The justification connects constraints to the tradeoff.

options.text: O(n log n) is always faster than O(n) because sorting has optimized libraries.
options.explanation: Asymptotic order does not support that claim.

options.text: Hashing is mathematically incorrect whenever collisions are possible.
Choose sorting because it is familiar, regardless of the stated constraints.
options.explanation: Familiarity is not a contract-based justification.

feedback.reason: A strategy justification should name the constraint that makes the tradeoff worthwhile.

blocks.text: The linear notation alone is not decisive when one bound is expected and the other deterministic. The chosen approach is justified by the required guarantee and available memory, not by library familiarity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_is_always_faster: Asymptotic order does not support that claim.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_familiar: Familiarity is not a contract-based justification.

items.prompt: Which sentence best justifies a two-pointer scan on a sorted array for a target pair?
constraints: The array is sorted.
The pointer movement must discard candidates safely.

options.text: If the current sum is too small, moving the left pointer right discards no solution using that left value; if too large, moving the right pointer left is symmetric.
options.explanation: This states the monotone elimination invariant.

options.text: Two pointers are appropriate because sorted arrays usually use two pointers.
options.explanation: Pattern association is not a proof.

options.text: The scan checks every pair explicitly, so no candidate is discarded.
options.explanation: The algorithm does discard pairs and must justify it.

options.text: Sorting guarantees a hash table is unnecessary for every pair problem.
options.explanation: The target relation and output contract still matter.

feedback.reason: A good justification explains why each pointer movement safely eliminates a region of candidates.

blocks.text: Sorted order turns the current sum comparison into a dominance fact: all pairs beyond one boundary are too large or too small. That is the proof behind linear movement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.looks_sorted: Pattern association is not a proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.try_all: The algorithm does discard pairs and must justify it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_needed: The target relation and output contract still matter.

items.prompt: How should a strategy justification explain that a frequency map is sufficient for a window constraint?
constraints: The predicate depends only on symbol multiplicities.
The window changes by adding right and removing left.

options.text: The map stores exactly the counts needed to decide validity, and each boundary update changes those counts without needing the full window history.
options.explanation: This establishes state sufficiency and update closure.

options.text: The map is sufficient because it stores every prior array position.
options.explanation: A frequency map stores aggregate counts, not all history.

options.text: The map is correct because frequency constraints are common in interviews.
options.explanation: The proof must connect state to the predicate.

options.text: The map works only after sorting the current window.
options.explanation: Sorting changes order and is unnecessary for multiplicity constraints.

feedback.reason: A state is justified by showing that it is sufficient for validity and closed under the algorithm's transitions.

blocks.text: If the predicate asks only about counts, adding and removing one symbol updates the complete decision state. If order or positions matter, the map alone is insufficient.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_everything: A frequency map stores aggregate counts, not all history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.validity_assumed: The proof must connect state to the predicate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_symbols: Sorting changes order and is unnecessary for multiplicity constraints.

items.prompt: What should a justification say when no candidate satisfies all constraints simultaneously?
constraints: Every known approach violates at least one contract dimension.
The user expects an honest decision.

options.text: State that the current constraints are mutually incompatible or require relaxing a specific dimension; do not present a violating strategy as compliant.
options.explanation: An explicit unavailable state preserves trust.

options.text: Choose the fastest approach and omit the constraint it violates.
options.explanation: Silent contract violations are not a valid strategy.

options.text: Add a metadata flag saying the approach is future-compatible.
options.explanation: Metadata does not make an invalid approach valid.

options.text: Present the approach as correct because it works on common inputs.
options.explanation: Common cases cannot satisfy a universal contract.

feedback.reason: A strategy choice is allowed to be unavailable when the constraints conflict; the justification should expose the exact conflict.

blocks.text: For example, an in-place O(1)-space requirement can conflict with preserving arbitrary input order and aliases. The correct response is to identify the required relaxation or ask for a changed contract, not to hide the violation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hide_violation: Silent contract violations are not a valid strategy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add_flag: Metadata does not make an invalid approach valid.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.average_cases: Common cases cannot satisfy a universal contract.
